challenges.name: latency-throughput-concurrency
challenges.title: Latency, throughput or concurrency?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the exam-day rehearsal: two k6 runs of the leaderboard endpoint with different numbers of virtual users, and a short request log. Decide what each one really shows.

questions.question:
Two k6 runs of GET /api/leaderboard on the staging API, closed loop (each VU waits for its response, then sends the next request), no think time, 120 s of steady state each:

# run A - 100 VUs
http_req_duration....: avg=82.4ms med=79.8ms p(95)=104.2ms
http_req_failed......: 0.00%  0 out of 145248
http_reqs............: 145248  1210.4/s

# run B - 300 VUs
http_req_duration....: avg=244.6ms med=241.0ms p(95)=281.7ms
http_req_failed......: 0.00%  0 out of 147000
http_reqs............: 147000  1225.0/s

Statement: "Run B shows that the leaderboard endpoint can serve about three times the load that run A measured, with no errors."
questions.explanation: False. Load served is throughput: completed requests per second. It went from 1210.4/s to 1225.0/s, about 1% more, while the number of requests in flight (the VUs) tripled. With throughput flat at the server's capacity, the extra concurrency can only turn into waiting time, and it did: 1225.0/s x 0.2446 s = 300 requests in flight, the 300 VUs, and the average latency tripled from 82 ms to 245 ms. The common misconception is to read VUs (concurrency) as capacity: three times the VUs means three times as many requests waiting, not three times as many served.

questions.question:
Five requests to POST /api/submissions recorded by the load generator (times in ms from the start of the test, all answered 201 Created):

request  start_ms  end_ms
A              0     300
B             50     900
C            200    1400
D            400     600
E            700    1100

The report computes throughput for the window from 0 ms (included) to 1000 ms (excluded).

Statement: "Throughput in this window is 3 requests per second: C and E were sent inside the window, but they do not count because they completed after it."
questions.explanation: True. Throughput counts requests that completed in the window: A (300 ms), B (900 ms) and D (600 ms), so 3 completions in 1 second. C and E were in flight during the window and count towards its concurrency (the average number of requests in flight is (300 + 850 + 800 + 200 + 300) / 1000 = 2.45), but their latency and their completion belong to the next window. The misconception is to count requests sent as throughput: a generator can send faster than the server completes, and the difference is a growing queue, not extra throughput.
